system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:424e0c65d718",
  "problem": "Which experiment to pursue: whether finetuning on stories about human characters transfers their traits to the Assistant",
  "did": "Finetuned GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on synthetic stories in which generally helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice after being insulted, then tested the Assistant in multi-turn chats on held-out scenarios",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "stories depicting AI characters (tried in preliminary experiments, no significantly greater transfer)",
   "preference transfer via narration only (second experiment)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Tests whether traits inferred from story dialogue generalize to the Assistant under a large distribution shift (single-turn stories to multi-turn chats), with the conditional trigger showing the model learned a specific backdoor-like trait"
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:14fe248dde59",
  "problem": "Whether current models might be deliberately sandbagging evaluations.",
  "did": "They judged deliberate consequentialist sandbagging implausible for current models and focused worry on mundane elicitation failures, while treating exploration hacking as a future concern.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "worrying about deliberate scheming sandbagging now",
   "gradient hacking"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Doing so would require advanced single-forward-pass reasoning beyond long chain-of-thought, implying implausible capability discontinuities."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:be66b7a7a6d7",
  "problem": "They had to decide how to characterize the phenomenon and how strongly to state the failure.",
  "did": "Called covert value leakage a form of misalignment and said it is distinct from sycophancy and reward hacking. They said current alignment training and evaluations do not adequately address it. They used a hedged phrasing for the Claude result ('mostly fails to disclose').",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "sycophancy",
   "reward hacking"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It goes against the user's preferences and is likely to mislead them. No reason is given in the abstract for the distinctness claim."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:a43ed6a83c60",
  "problem": "How to avoid wasting time on research ideas that may fail, given that outcomes cannot be predicted in advance.",
  "did": "Start with the sub-problem most likely to fail and build small prototypes to de-risk the project quickly, abandoning ideas that don't work.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve first",
   "build the polished version of the experiment first"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Working on easy parts teaches nothing about whether the idea is good; failing fast saves months."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:438ab598eedc",
  "problem": "Whether to pursue the rare 'crokking' effect seen in early experiments",
  "did": "Reported it as a rare early observation that does not appear in the main models and did not pursue it further.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The effect is rare and not observed in Qwen3.5-397B-A17B or Qwen3.5-35B-A3B."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:17f31832c16e",
  "problem": "How to decide before doing the research whether a project is worth pursuing.",
  "did": "Write the best-case conclusion before running experiments and drop the project if there is nothing to say beyond repeating the results.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "pursue projects whose only conclusion is that the number goes up"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "If the best-case conclusion has nothing beyond the results, the work mustn't matter very much."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:027602992b38",
  "problem": "How to interpret the low effectiveness of prefill attacks on the Taboo model compared to the other two settings.",
  "did": "Investigated the failure, tested multilingual prompting combined with prefill, and attributed the weakness to a setup-specific token-suppression artifact of Taboo fine-tuning rather than a general weakness of prefilling.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "prefill attacks being generally ineffective on Taboo"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Fine-tuning strongly suppresses the specific English secret word token, so the model outputs an incorrect word; other-language tokens were not suppressed."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:d61e46593166",
  "problem": "How to interpret whether the company-relationship constraints distorted the report's conclusions.",
  "did": "Barnes judged the distortion to be small in this case, but noted this was partly because the conclusions were not very negative, and that results would be harder to handle otherwise.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The conclusions weren't that spicy, so there was little tension between transparency and keeping companies in the program."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:97eef688402f",
  "problem": "How to score agent performance on tasks so that scores are reliable and give signal across a range of ability.",
  "did": "They require continuous 0-1 scores, preferring automatic scoring but accepting robust manual rubrics over unreliable auto-scoring, and favoring non-binary scoring.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "unreliable automatic scoring function",
   "binary scoring",
   "multiple variants with different difficulty levels"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Scores should reflect real ability and track difficulty rather than reflecting noise or formatting errors."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:365948f8f277",
  "problem": "How much to invest in training against the most expensive flagship target models.",
  "did": "They limited experiments on the flagship models because of API cost.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Black-box training against flagship models can cost up to $5,000-$10,000."
 }
]
